## 8. Wave-18 developer loop amendment (DX4)

Implementer: Codex for Charlie Cheever, 2026-10-19, wave-18 fixes #3/#4/#8.
SEC4 owns security campaigns and lint semantics; QRY owns read semantics.
MIG's staging clock is governed by LLP 3000.000.000.002 §4 and unchanged.

`seedAccounts` accepts `service` (default operator, same 1–64 character seat
validation as operatorToken) and merges `args(account)` over `{principal, role}`.
Explicit custom keys override defaults. It validates the seat before effects;
production/dev refusal still precedes mint/signup. Only the chosen service's
existing mutation authority applies. First-admin's tested guide authenticates
first, tries signup only after failed login, and calls the operator-only roster
upsert. Repetition preserves the principal and role; wrong credentials cannot
replace an account or grant. Bulk batches still create fresh random accounts.

Proof `startDev` echoes the closed-door guidance to caller stderr after matching
its per-launch /auth/config marker. Guides start/cheatsheet/personas surface
staging in the ordinary loop. No proof success is inferred from the notice.

Disposable dev already uses a private file/WAL store. It now retains an Owner
and publishes the identical mutual-HMAC/AEAD local token proof as persistent
dev. Locked, private project registry entries include an optional `storePath`.
`token --service` selects a unique live project entry; `--port N` selects among
entries (including closed-door password-only hosts). `--release` is exclusive
with --port. The selected path must still pass existing hardened auxiliary-file,
store-identity, live-owner and mutual-proof checks. Registry data alone grants no
authority; no bearer can mint and no unprotected token door is added. Multiple
hosts refuse implicit selection. Explicit unmatched ports refuse without
falling back to another store. Older records without a proof path request a
restart. Live minting uses the current host clock, matching session resolution
and staging, so time-travel dev does not mint already-expired tokens. Offline
minting retains wall time. Disposable directory ownership and cleanup last for
the whole host lifetime.

Session lifetimes stay seven days on the authoritative application clock.
Every successful or post-advance maintenance-failed clock reply includes a
sessionNotice explaining login after large jumps and upload after time travel;
the clock CLI and staging proof helper echo it on stderr. Reset replies state
that accounts/sessions were removed and cached credentials must be discarded,
then users recreated and roles reprovisioned. This deliberately preserves auth
expiry testing rather than silently extending credentials. Production keeps
its generic auth refusals. Staging's real throttles stay unchanged; the refusal
names Retry-After/retryAfterMs and seedAccounts. Dev loopback already has no
minute counters: scripted dev must serialize KDF work rather than raise a
nonexistent minute limit. This choice avoids a staging/production auth fork.

Upgrade scans bounded authored JS/TS/shell/JSON sources for /seed, /dev/*,
persona headers and startDev calls, skips dependencies/generated/store/output
folders and symlinks, prints per-project paths and migration actions even for
quiet/JSON callers, and returns warnings in JSON. A bounded/incomplete scan
says so. It reports candidates, not a claim that every listed startDev call
lacks --memory. Password-only doors closed and helper persistence began at
0.4.33; scanning also covers surviving risky scripts upgrading from 0.4.33.
Store-lock errors retain recorded PID/address and recommend disposable memory
proofs or stopping the recorded owner. Port conflict probes consult public
/auth/config when closed dev /dev/status refuses; they do not infer non-dev
from a 403.

Evidence: affected unit/native/client tests, packed guide recipes and DX4
cases in Linux consumer qualification; copied 5×wave18 and 5×wave17 upgrade
warning transcripts, assigned Mac Studio affected tests, full crate suites,
ref/docs budget and repository inventory/guide checks. Actual results and any
limits are in WORKSTREAM-REPORT.md; no publication claim or version bump.

DX4 review: [Muse READY](./reviews/dx4/r2-muse.txt) and
[fresh Codex READY](./reviews/dx4/r2-codex.txt) on the same amendment;
[commands, complete transcripts and source hashes](./reviews/dx4/provenance.json).


## 9. Wave-19 identity retry and local production lifecycle

Commission: Charlie's day-two addendum, wave-19 fixes #6/#7 (2026-10-19).
This amends the SDK/proof and local release contracts; it grants no new auth
or filesystem authority. SEC4 and QRY keep their existing scopes.

Identity `guest`, `signup` and `login` share a portable request helper with
proof `seedAccounts` (including `startServe({seedUsers})`). Only a delivered
HTTP 429 containing a validated auth `E_RATE_LIMIT` refusal, not marked
`retryable:false`, may retry. The server refuses these requests before account
creation/authentication. Wait for nonnegative integer `retryAfterMs`, or a
valid Retry-After header on older servers (otherwise one second). Preserve the
same credentials and scope, without sending retry options on the wire. Up to
four attempts fit inside the whole request deadline (`timeoutMs`, default
180000); an AbortSignal cancels fetch and waiting. A wait that cannot fit
returns the original refusal with its delay; setup instead throws
E_STAGING_TIMEOUT, warning that partial accounts/grants may remain. Setup
passes its remaining overall budget (default five minutes). There is no
polling at a fixed short interval. Transport errors, malformed responses,
other status/family/codes, permanent refusals, session rotations and role
provisioning mutations never automatically replay. Account/role admission,
peer/email/KDF limits and the staging-before-mint boundary stay unchanged.
These deadlines rely on the fetch implementation honoring AbortSignal, as the
standard fetch does. Custom fetch adapters must honor that contract too.

Deploy and rollback may wait up to five seconds to acquire the actual owner
flock before admission. Missing/unreachable address hints select bounded
waiting; a responsive listener selects the existing authenticated control
status path. If that read-only status fails while shutdown is underway, use
only the remaining acquisition budget, then reread status under the acquired
owner. Neither status nor an address/PID hint admits activation. A subsequent
activation request or ambiguous reply is never replayed automatically. The
exclusive flock, canonical inode/hardlink checks, private auxiliary files,
revision CAS and immutable-source validation remain authoritative. Prune and
other offline command semantics are unchanged. A surviving owner still
refuses E_STORE_BUSY; no process is signalled based on a hint.

`serve DIR --wait-stopped` exposes a five-second lock-release barrier for
callers retaining their own process handle. It requires an existing database,
opens only its existing hardened private owner sidecar, obtains an exclusive
flock and validates the named sidecar/database inode. It does not open SQLite,
create a deployment/sidecar, clear address metadata or signal a PID. No owner
sidecar means no named ownership exclusion. The documented sidecar removal
boundary of LLP 3000.019 §3.4 remains; this is a point-in-time barrier, not a
reservation against a future owner. Other serve flags refuse before effects.

Proof `startServe().stop()` first terminates/reaps the retained native child
through the existing bounded TERM/KILL path, then awaits this barrier, including
any watchdog-held descriptor during worker cleanup. Concurrent/repeated stops
share the in-flight/successful operation. Failure rejects, clears the cached
failure and allows a later barrier retry; it cannot falsely claim cleanup.
No new PID lookup or automatic stop of another owner is introduced. The proof
host stop allowance includes the native child and five-second store barrier.

`data TABLE --json` returns `{rows, more, limit}` for empty and nonempty
snapshots, replacing the bare array. `more` reports the existing one-extra-row
probe in the same read transaction, including default 50-row truncation and
`--limit 0`. Text JSON-lines and the stderr notice are preserved. This operator
surface still bypasses application read rules and refuses private/ephemeral
storage as before; no query semantics change. Existing repository consumers
and the 0.4.35 guide changes are updated for the envelope.

Required evidence: SDK/seed refusal timing, bounded attempts, cancellation and
non-replay tests; actual owner wait/no-effect probes; real delayed worker stop;
deploy/rollback cleanup with a still-listening stale control hint; JSON default
and explicit limit boundaries. Fresh packed Linux qualification must include
real server throttles and public SDK/seedUsers retry, production shutdown and
stdout-only inspection; affected Mac Studio lifecycle tests cover platform
sensitivity. Final exact results, review provenance and scoped limitations are
recorded in WORKSTREAM-REPORT.md.

## 10. Wave-20 loop repairs (DX5)

Commission: Charlie Cheever's wave-20 fix list #4, #6, #7, #8;
implementer Codex, 2026-10-21. This amendment is proposed until its two
independent reviews and implementation evidence are recorded. SEC5 owns
security intent, campaigns and exposure output; this lane changes lookup
advice, never the authority granted by an application rule.

### Clock reports

Amend LLP 3000.000.000.002 §4's proof helper return: `advance(duration)`
returns `{now, fired, held}`. Each entry carries the schedule name, target,
reason, boundary/window metadata and bounded run summary from the existing
operator-only schedule report. `now()` still returns a number. The CLI and
HTTP advance reply expose the same arrays, retaining `schedules` for existing
operator consumers. Fired means a schedule was enqueued, not that its job
succeeded; the run summary distinguishes parked or pending work. Every
non-fired schedule appears in held with a reason, including an already
processed boundary, a future saved boundary, initialization, a future window
or an explicit hold. Saved boundaries survive restart: one fire per boundary,
coalescing missed periods unless eachBoundary was explicitly requested.
The helper and CLI print saved-boundary holds and their recovery action on
stderr, including the equal-boundary case on a reused store. Advance never
rewinds markers or replays a completed boundary. Reply limits account for the
retained report plus its partition into fired/held. Staging's expiry notice
describes expiry/upload recovery without development-door instructions.
Ambiguous or failed advances are never retried; time may already have moved.
Maintenance failures return an explicitly incomplete schedule report with the
advanced time; the proof helper attaches this reply to its thrown error.

### Source diagnostics without an existence oracle

Extend LLP 3000.036.002 §15.2's N_LOOKUP_FILTERED advice to required reads
and reads of written tables. A later write and an asserted `! else CODE` do
not prove read authority. Existing key/flow proofs still suppress advice,
including prior successful exact reads and deliberately public projections.
One note names the source lookup, authored hiding rule, declaration and the
null/custom-refusal consequence; duplicate N_LOOKUP_HIDDEN notes at that
site are avoided (the more specific N_LOOKUP_HIDDEN takes precedence). This is missing-proof advice, not a claim every caller
is refused. Program `exists` and rule-witness `exists` keep distinct semantics.

For private tables with secondary unique keys, source advice explains that
an unreadable conflicting row uses generic E_RULE (or an undisclosed write
target miss), even when the unique declaration has `else CODE`. The named
constraint applies only when the conflict can be disclosed. Do not return
the declared code only on hidden conflicts: that would violate LLP 3000 §7
and LLP 3000.036.002 §15.2. Public E_RULE repair text, if changed, is identical
for ordinary rule rejection and hidden collision. No row, key, actual hiding
clause or hidden-dependent meter enters the public refusal. Rewrites propose
a minimal readable key projection or operator-mediated ownership/claim flow,
never broader disclosure of private rows. Paired hidden/missing lookup tests assert equality of public diagnostics and
logical meters. Hidden/ordinary write-refusal tests compare public refusals
and receipts; write replies expose no meter.

### Upgrade advice reaches the old CLI

Extend §8's bounded scan with candidate `data ... --json` consumers in authored
scripts, including argv-array and shell forms. List paths without printing
source. State the one-line migration `JSON.parse(stdout).rows` for the former
bare array, and preserve `more`/`limit`. This is a candidate scan, not an AST
proof or an automatic rewrite; report scan limits.

The installed wrapper runs project warnings before the first ordinary check
for that installed version, independently of the runtime-history receipt.
A warning receipt is written only after delivery to a terminal (or an empty
scan). Piped/captured stderr cannot establish delivery: old quiet upgrades
discard it, so a nonempty scan stays unacknowledged and the next ordinary
check repeats the advice, including in CI. Baseline checks neither deliver
nor acknowledge warnings; read/receipt failures do not fail compilation.
Warnings always use stderr, preserving one-object JSON stdout and quiet-mode
visibility. This reaches the usual published 0.4.33/0.4.35 upgrade path because
their upgrade invokes the newly installed wrapper for check. A fresh-process
resolution must select new bytes after package replacement. Direct upgrade
keeps its existing pre-install warning behavior. Test both published old CLIs
against the fresh packed package in an isolated local registry, including
--quiet and --json --quiet and the deferred first check; do not claim
an upgrade was tested by invoking only the new helper.

### Frontend and starter custody

Extend LLP 3000.013.002 §2 with `ReadState` in snapback4/react: a list read
(or PageHook) renders loading, denied, empty, or authorized data through one
component. It adds no subscription, cache or authority. It preserves partial
and stale rows; empty means the returned list is empty, never proven absence.
Loading and empty default to null; denied uses the supplied renderer or
throws the existing QueryRefusal for an error boundary. Children receive the
typed list and precise settled read metadata. Browser and React Native
callers supply their own display elements.

The Expo adapter owns `snapback4-expo/metro` (CommonJS withSnapback(config))
and its wasm transformer. Resolve Expo's transformer relative to the consuming
project/config, compatible with isolated package-manager installs. Preserve
the caller's config and append the existing .snapback4 block and wasm support.
New starter Metro config only obtains Expo's default and calls withSnapback.
The adapter also owns the native smoke sign-in hook; new starters import it
instead of carrying src/native-smoke.ts. Password and guest selection remain
explicit; ordinary launches never sign in automatically. Old modified helpers
remain app-owned. No native engine or simulator custody changes.

Amend LLP 3000.011.003.000 §7.2: adapt replaces an untouched todo frontend
proof with a runnable proof scaffold retaining frontend:proof/proof:web and
Playwright. It starts the correct frontend and checks rendered content, then
explicitly refuses to claim an app-specific write proof until the builder
adds one. A custom proof is never rewritten. Fresh non-todo starters get the
same scaffold. Every Expo starter includes playwright-core, including custom
schemas. Qualification runs changed guide/starter sources from the packed
tarball, tests the expected scaffold refusal, and records frontend character
reductions on copies of three wave-20 Expo lanes. No original lane is edited.

### Acceptance and scope

Full five-crate Rust tests, affected client tests, fresh-pack Linux consumer
qualification with per-item cases and published-old-CLI upgrades, Mac Studio
affected platform tests, ref-check, docs budget and repository-root checks.
No test.sh, publication, push or version bump is authorized by this work.
WORKSTREAM-REPORT.md records exact commands/results, commits and limitations;
review transcripts and source provenance live in llp/reviews/dx5/.

Gotchas you cannot derive from the code:

- Own Cargo and Bun workspaces; the repository root excludes them. Run cargo/bun from `snapback4/`. Node 24.x (`engines`): run the suite with the pinned runtime on PATH, not the ambient Homebrew node.
- Web builds require `bun install --frozen-lockfile` first. Binaryen 132.0.0 is
  an exact workspace devDependency; build/measurement invoke its portable
  `node_modules/binaryen/bin/wasm-opt` through Node, never a PATH optimizer.
  Missing/mismatched dependencies and optimizer failures refuse the build.
  See README's web-device build instructions and HV round 4 for host parity.
- The suite schedules client files in one pool: `max(1, min(24,
  floor(os.availableParallelism() / 3)))` slots (3 on 10 CPUs, 24 on 96).
  This counts Linux CPU affinity and leaves room for each file's servers,
  browser renderers and workers. Acquisition and server-e2e share that pool;
  there are no extra shard processes outside it. Real-timer files listed in
  `TIMER_CLIENT_FILES` drain that pool and run individually afterward with
  unchanged timing bounds. The quote-jump browser witness remains pooled.
  The two full-count model
  files retain a separate serial slot. `SNAPBACK4_TEST_SERIAL_CLIENT_FILES=1`
  still forces one client file at a time. The external file watchdog measures
  time since a subtest started or finished: max(900 seconds, largest single
  declared guard + max(60 seconds, 25%)). There is no absolute duration cap.
  Console output does not count as progress. Serial mode uses the same bounds.
  See `scripts/run-client-tests.mjs` and the QF round-2 guard census; update
  named work counts and recheck the census when declarations change. Every
  file runs as native `node --test` with default isolation, in a process group
  whose first member is a tiny Node keeper. The runner closes the keeper's stdin
  on completion, stall or abort; only the keeper calls `kill(0, SIGKILL)`.
  Runner death also closes that pipe. An unexpectedly exited keeper fails the
  file and never authorizes a runner signal. Cleanup requires two consecutive
  completed inspections (50 ms apart) with no living group member. Observed leftovers
  fail as TEST_FILE_LEAK. Failed listings and unclassifiable PID/PPID/PGID
  prefixes remain fail-closed. A ps timeout at two seconds retries once with a
  60-second bound; all other command errors refuse immediately. Listings use
  asynchronous spawn so other files' timers and keeper EOF delivery keep running.
  File watchdogs and cleanup's five-second window use per-file monotonic time.
  Expiry requires another completed snapshot: a live group after the deadline
  refuses; two consecutive empty snapshots pass even when the second is late.
  Precisely
  recognized exit-time routing anomalies
  discard the whole snapshot and retry at most twice, 50 ms apart; persistent
  anomalies refuse and never confer ownership (LLP 3000 §7, QF2).
  Metadata is validated for group members and
  their visible descendants; unrelated rows only increment diagnostics.
  Signed Darwin UIDs, variable lstart spacing and comm spaces are accepted.
  Vanished members count as exited. Processes leaving the group (setsid,
  setpgid or detached spawns) are outside cleanup custody; visible descendants
  receive metadata validation but are never signalled by the runner. Native Node's exit
  status alone decides test success; reporter counts are diagnostic only.
  The reporter observes progress as Node delivers it: synchronous work that
  does not yield may buffer events in Node's child until that work finishes.
  Such an unreported interval is subject to the same stall bound. See QF Round 7.
  The M5 MacBook is the publication host; the office M1 is calibration-only.
- Client tests and their helpers must gate Linux APIs (`/proc`, `strace`, `ss`,
  `taskset`, namespace/network tools) at the test or call, or implement a
  portable fallback. Keep portable assertions running on Darwin and give each
  skipped witness an explicit reason. The client pool runs
  `test-platform-audit.test.mjs`: a cheap static census follows static named/namespace `.mjs`
  imports and named helpers and checks scoped Linux skips/branches/early returns.
  A gate in another test does not count. This conservative common-case guard
  does not prove dynamic imports, generated scripts or arbitrary control flow;
  review those paths and run affected tests on the publication Mac.
  Listener snapshots and syscall tracing are Linux qualification capabilities,
  never dependencies of the published `snapback4/proof` browser helper.
- Before a publication dry run, warm the test artifacts **in that publication
  worktree**, while the host is free of calibration work:
  `LIBSQLITE3_FLAGS=-USQLITE_ENABLE_MEMORY_MANAGEMENT cargo test --workspace --no-run`.
  Use the dry run's toolchain, target directory, profile/features, `RUSTFLAGS`
  and Cargo profile environment. Do not add `--release` or `--profile production`:
  the suite uses the default test profile. The suite still asks Cargo for the
  complete test inventory, runs every binary and runs doctests separately.
  Warming compiles without executing tests and supplies no qualification receipt.
- One owner on the core (LLP 3000 decision 4): the engine, the store and the client contract are written by the lead session; Codex lanes take the fixture generator, the reference apps, the device witnesses and the periphery. Do not reshape `contract.ts` from a lane; propose the change in the journal.
- No ceiling is raised in slice one (LLP 2000.000 §12). A thing that does not fit changes the design or waits.
- The journal is append-only and dated; never rewrite an entry. LLP 3000 §7 carries decisions that must outlive it.
- Nothing here depends on `snapback2/` at runtime. Copy source deliberately, split under 1,500 lines on the way in, and say so in the journal.
- Named lane: `~/projects/snapback-sb4` on `sb4/*` branches. Never `git stash`; commit checkpoints.
- The conformance corpus (`corpus/`) is Snapback 2's serialized IR and value
  model; the core keeps those serializations so it binds. A case the slice
  cannot run is skipped with a named reason, never counted as a pass.
- `snapback/generated/api.ts` is built by `check` and `dev`, never committed;
  the app's typecheck needs a `check` first (the suite does one).
- Point rule probes and `exists` require a unique key. A fully pinned superset
  of a required unique key is unique too (for example an explicit role index
  containing the unique conversation/principal pair). Nullable unique key
  arguments need non-null proof. Other existence checks use bounded populations
  in code. Named equalities covering a total unique key check extra columns on
  that one row without an additional index.
- The packaged CLI uses `LIBSQLITE3_FLAGS=-USQLITE_ENABLE_MEMORY_MANAGEMENT` during both publication tests and its production build (LLP 3000 §7). A plain production Cargo build retains the dependency's ordinary SQLite policy; use the same build input when comparing with the package. The variable is unnecessary at runtime.
- When creating a stage, `scripts/publish.mjs` runs the suite and refuses on red, builds the production binary, packs `snapback4-darwin-arm64` and verifies the installed digest, then publishes both packages. Bump `version` in `packages/snapback4/package.json` (and its `optionalDependencies`), `packages/snapback4-darwin-arm64/package.json`,
  `packages/snapback4-linux-x64/package.json` and `Cargo.toml` together; a test refuses a mismatch.
- Publication retains exact qualified tarballs under `target/publication/`. If a
  stage exists, use `node scripts/publish.mjs --resume` to validate its recorded
  suite qualification, requalify those exact bytes through the installed-consumer
  proof, and finish missing registry artifacts; an existing version must match
  its staged integrity. This also applies after `--dry-run`. An ordinary invocation
  refuses an existing stage so changed source cannot silently publish old bytes.
  Bump the version to build a new pair; preserve a partially published stage.
- Cross-host publication (LLP 3000.021 §3.3): prepare the common client once
  from clean release source, qualify that tarball on Linux, and import the
  Linux tarball plus its receipt on the Mac. Source commit, client SRI and
  Linux SRI must agree. Linux prefers working Docker/Podman, otherwise uses checksum-pinned proot
  with clean Ubuntu 24.04/Alpine root filesystems in a user cache, and refuses
  `NPM_TOKEN` or `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN`, even when empty. It never signs or packs
  the client. The Mac never rebuilds or executes Linux; `--resume` rechecks
  its copied receipt. No receipt packs a Darwin-only client; an existing
  two-platform preparation is refused on that path. Packed dependencies must
  match the staged set. Uploads use verified private snapshots, with each
  digest checked again immediately before publish.
  Commands and current qualification limits:
  [`reports/20260927-lx-linux-package/REPORT.md`](./reports/20260927-lx-linux-package/REPORT.md).
- The guide is tested text. Every ```quarry block in `crates/snapback4-lang/src/guide.rs` and in `packages/snapback4/README.md` is compiled by `crates/snapback4-lang/tests/guide.rs` with no diagnostic and no note (the language card is also run against the engine); every refusal code the sources emit must be in `guide::CODES`; every `guide("..")` a diagnostic carries must name a card. Add a form to the language card when you add it to the parser, fence README Quarry as ```quarry, and never fence Quarry as plain text to dodge the test.
- Native jobs (LLP 3000.005) need `rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown`; the suite's fixture build fails loudly without it. The guest SDK `crates/snapback4-native` is a path dependency until it is published; an app's `snapback/native/Cargo.toml` names it by path.

Quarry store testing (LLP 3000.035 §5.1): `SNAPBACK4_EVAL_POSTGRES` is an
explicit evaluation connection. The factory owns one physical schema per worker,
restores its rows and bookkeeping, installs the compiled fixture, then opens the
ordinary engine. Mutation attempts restore a seeded snapshot; shrinking reuses
that same factory. `Database::connect_fresh()` is an opt-in test mode. Fresh and
restored outcomes must serialize to identical bytes. The local wire observer
retains SQLSTATE, message, detail and SQL statement before the public query API
converts a driver error to a refusal; it never changes the traffic.

Reads sweep every public boundary. Mutations compare every discovered position
twice on SQLite, and compare up to eight seeded positions per dimension on
Postgres (including first/last), plus the case's original budget. Sampling
counters are in `store_stats`; each selected position runs prefetch on and off.
Physical prefetch counters are separate from the exact public outcome record.
The widened generator (`src/widen.rs`) emits prefetch-reachable reads: pages
projecting `tags[.tag]` and `tags[name = .label]` (a `Get` and a unique
`Lookup` whose keys vary across rows) and a loop reading `tags[row.tag]`, so
`store_stats` reports marked reads, transferred rows, cases with a transfer
and `prefetch_consumption_witness_probes` (fewer database calls with prefetch
on: cached answers were consumed). A planted cached-hit-to-miss fault is caught
by the random corpus (LLP 3000.035 §5.1; the closed
[coverage ticket](../issues/closed/20261007-quarry-store-oracle-prefetch-coverage-gap.md)).
Heap is charged identically on every store and the device (LLP 3000.007
§20.24.5); any disagreement is a ticket candidate, never normalized into a pass.
The cluster regression asserts it finds no signature and refuses any new one.

`run-stores --seconds N` stops each worker between cases after N seconds; a case
and any shrinking already underway finish. `cases` remains the requested count,
`generated` is actual completed generation, and `time_limited_workers` reports
the early stop. Slowest-case timing includes generation, comparisons, shrinking
and artifact saving. It does not silently claim the requested million. The scheduled
runner rejects incomplete reports; its own `--hours` option instead chooses a
case count from a 256-case calibration of both campaigns, with 20% headroom and
a million-case cap. This is a sizing estimate, not a hard deadline.

Generator widening (`src/widen.rs`, LLP 3000.035 §5.1): from a stream
independent of the base generator (`generate::base`; a seed it leaves alone is
the base case byte for byte), cases gain prefetch-reachable reads, mutation
blocks (lets, `require`, `if`, several writes to `key` and `k2`, reads after
writes), a prelude of mutations `prep0..` run in order on the same store before
`run` (`Case::steps`, sometimes as the other viewer; `observe` then reads both
keys), and expiry (`expire at .until`, a clock advancing from `seeded_at`
through each step to `clock`, sweeps, `until: now + ttl`). Every oracle runs the
prelude (`execute::world`) and compares its outcomes (`prelude-*` fields;
`store-postgres-prelude`); a device acquires at the seed clock and catches up by
one sync round after the server's prelude. The prelude is emitted first so no
rewrite moves its sites. `lean::generate` narrows half the cases outside the
model (projections, expiry) back into its fragment; the rest stay named
unsupported (`shape`, `loop`, `table-expiry`). The report's `coverage` counts
each new feature (`block/*`, `prelude/*`, `projection/*`, `expire/*`, `clock/*`).

Quarry device testing (`src/devices.rs`, `src/device_writes.rs`, LLP 3000.035
§5.1 oracle 4): each case runs on a server engine and on a device of each store
(native SQLite at a file path, and memory), both brought up through the client's
own path: the `/schema` backend as JSON text, then `local.ts::syncRound` (capture
`sync_state`, `/sync` snapshot pages built as `serve_sync.rs` builds them,
`observe_store`, `apply` through `call_text`, catch-up stream). Never seed a
device store directly. Reads the device publishes without the server (`complete`
with `unknown` false, or a known refusal) compare the whole outcome record
except `seq` (and server-only `delivery`); every other read counts under a named
reason (`online-only-*`). Low ceilings reach the device only through `call`'s
`spent` ledger (`default - n`), compared at the server's boundary positions.
Writes go through `admit`: a device refusal must equal the server's, a
predicted row must equal the committed one (less its `pending` marker), and
after `settle` plus a sync round the device must answer `observe` as the server
does. `run-devices` accepts `--seconds`. Known findings are retained under
`cases/found/device-*` with a `DIAGNOSIS.md`; `tests/devices.rs` replays them
and `tests/smoke.rs` pins the fixed-seed signature set.

The Lean oracle (`run-lean`, LLP 3000.035 §5.2): `snapback4_lang::emit::lean`
translates each generated program's surface tree (never the binder's IR) to
the model's case JSON; `quarry-oracle` (`lean/Oracle.lean`, one process per
worker) answers one tagged outcome per line; the engine runs on SQLite at
default ceilings. Compared: kind, refusal code, data (tagged: an id is not a
text), `complete`, `next` presence, each side's own continuation, and a
mutation's `observe` reread. Not compared: meter fields and sites. Programs
outside the model's fragment are named unsupported reasons, never passes.
`lean::generate` adds Lean-only variants (per-effect rules, a hidden probe
target, nullable/id orders, residual filters) aimed at `lean/OPEN.md`. A
disagreement is a Rust defect, a model defect (only when a document
contradicts the model: fix the model, rerun `lean/check.sh`), or an open
point (record the engine's behaviour in `OPEN.md`); never change the model to
match the engine without a document. Findings live in
`cases/found/lean--*` with `DIAGNOSIS.md`; `tests/lean.rs` replays them and
pins the open signature set. Lean-dependent tests skip loudly without the
built model; `SNAPBACK4_REQUIRE_LEAN=1` makes that a failure.

Quarry scheduled testing: prepare a separate clean clone whose current branch
can fast-forward to `origin/main`. The runner fetches/fast-forwards it and starts
its own socket-only evaluation cluster with `fsync=off`,
`synchronous_commit=off`, `full_page_writes=off`, `shared_buffers=1GB`, and
`max_connections=200`. It builds the Lean model's `quarry-oracle` first
(`lake build` in `lean/`; a host without `lake` fails the run), then runs the
SQLite, store, device and Lean campaigns on the selected
seed window, replays shrunk findings twice, and files/appends open `issues/*.md`
tickets. Only ticket changes are committed/pushed, with three fetch/rebase
retries. State and reports live outside Git under `--state-dir`; seeds advance
only after completed work and successful owned-cluster cleanup. Dirty/diverged
trees, overlap, setup failures, partial reports and failed publication refuse.
A crash can retain the lock and cluster directory; inspect `lock/owner.json`
and the run report. Never stop a cluster by process name.

`--dry-run --cases 32` writes previews and a separate `next-seed.dry-run.json`,
never commits or pushes. Dry runs may explicitly supply `--external-postgres
'host=... user=... dbname=...'`; that cluster is neither started nor stopped by
the runner. Ambient connections do not override normal private-cluster ownership.
The installer remains an operator action; do not invoke it during development.

The Lean oracle on a scheduled host (one-time, per user, no sudo): install
elan with `curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leanprover/elan/master/elan-init.sh -sSf | sh -s -- -y --default-toolchain none`.
The runner finds `lake` on `PATH` or in `~/.elan/bin`; the first `lake build`
downloads the toolchain pinned in `lean/lean-toolchain` (Lean 4.34.1, no
Mathlib), so the first scheduled run needs network. Check by hand with
`(cd lean && ./check.sh)` in the runner's clone. `run.json` records the pinned
toolchain and the oracle binary's digest.
# What Snapback 4 Does Not Do

Longer than the doing-list on purpose. Moving something off it means writing one
line naming what it unblocks and taking something off the doing-list in the same
change. Nothing comes off during slice one (LLP 3000 §3: the clock is four weeks).

## The bars

The bakeoff gates in [LLP 3000 §3](../llp/3000-snapback4.explainer.md) are the
bars: the loop bar, hub acquisition within 2× the measured floor, client bytes
under the competitor-anchored budgets, the six scenarios green in the simulator
on the hub fixture. Everything not required to pass them does not exist yet.

## Not building

- **A second authoring language.** Quarry, one spelling, copied from Snapback 2 (LLP 1004, LLP 1007 §4b). TypeScript is for seeds, journeys, effect bodies and the client.
- **Byte- and step-priced certification.** No closure, heap, output or step ceilings at `check`; the certificate certifies shape, uniformity, completeness class and prediction eligibility. Resources are metered at runtime (LLP 2000.000 §6).
- **A per-query result cache.** No range receipts, validators, halos, absence evidence, coverage spans, extent facts, held directories, fact integrity or swap journals. The client replicates declared partitions with one watermark each (LLP 2000.000 §7).
- **Engine-minted ids for client inserts, grants, ID slices.** Ids are client-minted, time-ordered, 128-bit; the engine mints for its own writes.
- **The `drain` protocol, follower-tab inbox rows, `defineItems`, `withHistory`, `mutationTarget`, `receipt.source`, `local.caughtUp`, `partial` reason codes.** The card (`packages/snapback4/src/contract.ts`) is the whole client vocabulary; `why` carries the rest.
- **`retain` as a receipt rule.** `until-revoked` and `delivered-history` survive as the client's leave policy on a scope tombstone.
- **JavaScript in the data plane.** Queries and mutations run in the Rust interpreter inside the SQLite transaction, and in the same interpreter on the client (host decided at week 3 by measurement, LLP 2000.000 §9). A *job* may be the app's own Rust, hosted as wasm through the interpreter's operations under the job's meter (LLP 3000.005, the Moves line below); a query or mutation may not.
- **An embedded JS engine for effects.** The data plane never calls out. `emit` writes the effect durably in the mutation's commit and an external worker holding a service token claims, performs and settles it over the wire (`snapback4/worker`); the four reference effects run on the builder's Node (LLP 2000.000 §10, decided 2026-09-13).
- **Committed generated code; an auth mode; a supervised bundler.** As Snapback 2 (`rules/NOT-DOING.md`): types by inference, personas not modes, `SNAPBACK_URL` is the client contract.
- **A TypeScript twin of the interpreter.** Retired by the author's ruling of 2026-09-13 (LLP 3000 §7): one implementation, in Rust, on every host — the core's SQLite under the native module, memory under wasm on the web with the host persisting each commit's changes. The web pays 312,924 B gzip before the diet where the twin's tier paid 16,842; the conformance obligation between two interpreters ends. Expo Go runs the online tier.
- **More than one hosted target, an admin console, media transcoding or thumbnails, push delivery itself (a worker's), cron syntax beyond `every N at HH:MM`, vector or relevance-ranked search (word-prefix search is in: `words(..)` and `matching`), federation, multi-region, device-to-device sync, at-rest encryption claims.** After the clock, on evidence.
- **General observability beyond `why`, `trace`, `logs`, `data`, `sql`, server operation latency, and bounded client subscription inspection.** The `sql` verb is read-only inspection of the developer's own store (LLP 3000.007 §8.8), never an application surface. Separately declared application SQL reads are admitted for increment D (LLP 3000.009 §6.2, §14.4; the 2026-09-16 Moves line below), not implemented by this inspection verb.
- **A guide corpus.** The compiler's facts, one language card and keyword cards, as Snapback 2; no freshness dates. Every card's Quarry is compiled by the suite and the language card is run, so a card cannot promise a form the parser refuses.

- **Partial union delivery, two group audiences, a public branch.** A union syncs principal-column branches and at most one group branch, each a whole disjunct of the read rule (LLP 3000.036.000.000); a branch with an extra condition, a second group or a `public` branch is refused with the rewrite, never partially delivered; service grants add no device audience (LLP 3000.007 §20.6). A union does not combine with delivered history, read-through children, synced or row-keyed views, owner keys, timelines, private field owners, acquisition windows or direct/inherited expiry on content or membership scopes.
- **Exact horizon maintenance.** The horizon bounds acquisition (a snapshot, a bootstrap); the log never evicts or back-fills to hold a device's group at exactly N rows. A local read past the acquired horizon by key says `complete: false`.

- **Clock expressions in rules.** A read rule compares with `=` and `!=` only; `.expiresAt > now` remains a mutation `require`. Stored lifetimes use `not before .col` for server-controlled opening and `expire at .col` for expiry. The engine publishes opening commits; devices receive no unopened payload. The supported compositions and explicit exclusions are in LLP 3000.036.003.
- **A jobs framework.** No priorities, worker pools or dead letters: one FIFO of runs, one chunk at a time, a refused chunk parked with its refusal. Actions, effects and scheduled actions carry per-operation retries, deadlines and cancellation, and a record per external step (LLP 3000.009 §5.2; the Moves line below). Missed period boundaries while a server is down fire once on return, not once per missed period.
- **Asset processing.** No transcoding, thumbnails, rungs or HEIC: the bytes are served as uploaded; JPEG, PNG, WebP and MP4 only; image dimensions and optional MP4 duration read from the header; MP4 dimensions are not extracted.
- **Search beyond word prefixes.** One tokenizer (NFC, lowercase, alphanumeric words), one index shape (`scope, words(cols), order.., id`), one read (`matching`): every term a prefix of some word, the first term's words merged as lanes, bounded by the meter in a uniform scope, at most 32 words in an admitted non-uniform scope. No stemming, no ranking by relevance, no phrase or mid-word matching, no per-language folding, no intersection index for the second term (it filters the page).
- **An identity provider.** Guests, password accounts, service seats, and sessions a service mints for accounts the application authenticated itself. No phone, OAuth, magic links or MFA in the engine: an application's worker verifies those and mints the session.
- **No multi-server presence, no presence history or last-seen storage, no broadcast event stream, no connection-bound rows.** `connected[p]` stays server-wide, counting held polls and their 35 s grace; a live query that may read it re-runs in the background about every 5 seconds to stay current (LLP 3000.018). Typing and viewing use short-lived, authorized ephemeral tables in one server process (LLP 3000.017); they never sync or decide durable invariants. A device does not know presence and says so.

## Process not doing

- **2026-09-28 — ordinary mixed search** (LLP 3000.028 §3.3, lane OS round 1).
  Admit the SDK's bounded merge of current server rows and certified Left images
  for the proved single time-ordered word page. This removes application-owned
  online/held selection for that shape. One server call per requested page;
  recomputation pays again from consumed positions. The coordinator shares the
  existing device read allowance. No durable search session, extra synced rows,
  new authority or additional allowance is admitted.

- **2026-09-28 — inferred current-scope word search** (LLP 3000.028 §3.3,
  lane OS). A single bare ordinary word page may derive the exact non-expiring
  membership audience for the existing compact server plan. This removes the
  requirement to repeat that audience predicate in this narrow server query.
  The compiler supplies a scoped words index when absent; it is an ordinary
  schema index, maintained on writes and on devices, with no extra synced rows
  or new authority. The device keeps its original bare scan. Round 0 left ordered composition
  and combined accounting outside its independent subset; round 1 above admits
  that bounded SDK composition. Durable search sessions remain excluded.
- **2026-10-12 — union sync audiences** (LLP 3000.036.000.000, workstream UNION, two blind review rounds). A table syncs to the union of principal-column audiences and one group audience; a device holds a row while any branch admits its viewer. What it unblocks: owner-or-team, buyer-or-seller and owner-or-staff tables offline for every reader, the shape three app farms asked for. Taken off: "one `sync` audience per table". Partial delivery, two groups and a public branch stay excluded (above).
- **2026-09-28 — explicit owner-key coverage** (LLP 3000.028 §3.4, Lane OK commission). A public window may opt into a compiler-owned, horizon-free principal key partition to answer ordinary own-key existence offline. Taken off: the exclusion of narrower platform key distribution beside one public window. General union audiences, full own-row replication and per-query absence caches remain excluded. The projection uses existing metered maintains, adoption and whole-partition publication; existing windows do not expand.
- **2026-09-26 — a live query keeps presence current** (LLP 3000.018). A 0.4.2 probe found an observed `connected[p]` reporting `fresh: true` while stale for over a minute, and a comparative builder polled around it. What it unblocks: online marks and presence-aware lists that stay current. Taken off: "a presence stream" as an exclusion for live queries; a presence API, last-seen storage and multi-server presence stay out. Under the author's standing authorization for reworks that make queries excellent (2026-09-25).

- **No drift registries, inventories, line-pinned diagnostics registries, claim digests or frozen-record gates.** Generated projections are built, not committed.
- **No gate bound to an exact commit; no push gated on a battery.** Five blocking checks in sixty seconds, run before push; everything slower on a schedule with bounded tickets.
- **No ceiling raised in slice one.** Budgets are anchored to a competitor's measured number and recorded once in the journal.
- **No standing panel** except the two blind reviews LLP 3000 decision 4 names (partition inversion; the meter's cut on non-uniform scans). The author explicitly commissioned the one-off LLP 3000.008 panel and disjoint Astra implementation lanes on 2026-09-14; its bounded disposition is recorded in that umbrella and LLP 3000 §7.
- **No new LLP number** without first extending LLP 3000 or LLP 2000.000; no spec without running code (`rules/RULES.md`: only implemented specs bind).
- **No second session on the core** during slice one; lanes take the periphery.
- **No test matrix as the primary harness.** The simulator is; real-browser and device witnesses cover only what it cannot reach.
- **No files over 1,500 lines**, including ones copied from Snapback 2. Split on
  the way in. The one exception is the package's published documents
  (`packages/snapback4/README.md` and its linked references): the rule exists to
  keep a *source* file reviewable, and the 0.2.25 calibration measured the cost of
  applying it to a document — splitting the README was that run's single largest
  scoring loss, because the builder then had four places to look instead of one
  (LLP 3000.007 §20.19). A published document is bounded by whether a builder can
  find one way in, not by a line count; the census that enforces this rule covers
  source, and says so.

## Deliberately worse

- No compatibility with Snapback 1 or Snapback 2 apps, packages or on-disk formats.
- No API stability before the clock; every publish is `0.0.x`.
- Sparse prose documentation; the diagnostics and the recipes carry the load.
- One hosted target, one platform binary at a time. SQLite remains the default store; Postgres as a production store is being built under LLP 3000.009.001 (Moves, 2026-10-20) and is not yet a supported deployment target.

## Moves

- **2026-10-20 — Snapback 4 on Postgres moves onto the doing-list** (author: "commit and push these things, then do your \"what i'd do next\" things, then get this working on postgres and measure it"; LLP 3000.009.001 and its children). Unblocks: the store-port extraction on SQLite (P0, including the `Committer` seam with the serial batch); the Postgres adapters for every durable-state family and `serve`/`deploy`/`doctor` over Postgres (P1), with store-held fencing, the declared HA mode and `BlobStore`; the optimistic committer, commissioned on 2026-10-19 and built after its execution stage is sized; the scale program of LLP 3000.009.001.002 with its raw-Postgres, Supabase and Convex controls on fleet machines; and a research note comparing replicated SQLite with Postgres for applications that outgrow one SQLite file. Taken off in the same change: the evaluation-only framing of the Postgres adapter. Stands: no publication or managed-service deployment authority, no lowering of Quarry to SQL, no SQL writes to managed data, one core owner. Several serving processes (P2), log retention, live graduation (LLP 3000.009.001.001) and the async-safe external anchor each wait for their own Moves line.

- **2026-10-13 — stored lower lifetimes (`not before`) are commissioned by PAGE2** (LLP 3000.036.003). This unblocks timed disclosure without an application publication job. Per-application jobs that flip a publication flag leave this admitted path; clock expressions in rules, captured lower lifetimes for read-through children, and boundary recounts for maintained data remain excluded. HS owns handshake transport; PAGE2 declares the new semantic capability.

  state for this one expiring read. General result caches, resumable queries,

### The physical floors (LLP 3000 §5, week 1)

Machine: Apple M5 Max, 128 GB, macOS 26.6.2; Node 24.18.0 (`node:sqlite`,
bundled SQLite); Chromium from the Playwright cache (`chromium-1243`), headless.
Rows are the frozen Clique scale log's own text sends (`floors/rows.mjs`):
99,090 messages across 901 conversations, about 204 bytes per row as a
partition-log envelope. Scripts under `floors/`; each prints one JSON line.

| Floor | What | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. One response | 10,000 envelopes as JSON | 2.04 MB raw; gzip-6 207 KB in 6.7 ms; gzip-9 189 KB in 36 ms; brotli-5 103 KB in 12 ms |
| 1. One response | all 99,090 envelopes | 20.3 MB raw; gzip-6 2.0 MB in 59 ms; brotli-5 1.18 MB in 92 ms |
| 2. IndexedDB write | 10,000 rows, one transaction (message + log row each) | 197 ms |
| 2. IndexedDB write | the same 10,000 rows as 200 transactions of 50 | 197 ms |
| 2. IndexedDB write | 99,090 rows in chunks of 5,000 | 2,270 ms |
| 2. IndexedDB read | one thread page of 50 through the compound index | 0.6 ms |
| 3. SQLite write (native, WAL) | 10,000 rows, one transaction | 31 ms (`synchronous=NORMAL`), 22 ms (`FULL`) |
| 3. SQLite write | the same as 200 transactions of 50 | 46 ms (`NORMAL`), 49 ms (`FULL`) |
| 3. SQLite write | 99,090 rows in 20 transactions | 375 ms |
| 4a. Local query, JS | index build over 99,090 rows; thread page via the index; full-scan page; body substring search | 5.7 ms; 0.14 µs; 1.1 ms; 2.8 ms (heap +12.7 MB) |
| 4b. Local query, SQLite | thread page via `byConvTime`; `count(*)`; `LIKE` scan | 26 µs; 1.0 ms; 5.9 ms |
| 5. Send fan-out | 1 message + 1 partition-log row + 50 recipient-log rows, one durable transaction | 0.15 ms per send (`NORMAL`), 0.34 ms (`FULL`) |

What the floors say. Acquiring 10,000 messages is bounded below by about
7 ms to compress, 200 KB on the wire, and 200 ms to write on the web or
30 ms on native SQLite: roughly a quarter of a second on the web and well
under a tenth on a phone before rendering. Snapback 2's measured 28.4 s for
the same content sits about 140× above the web floor and about 900× above
the native one; the 2× target LLP 3000 §3 sets is therefore about 0.5 s on
web and 0.1 s native for the 10,000-row tier, to be restated for the hub
principal's full partition once its horizon is chosen. A 50-member send
costs a third of a millisecond durably; fan-out on write is not the cost.

Not measured: `expo-sqlite` on a device or simulator (floor 3 uses native
SQLite through Node as its stand-in; the Expo witness lane should confirm
the constant in week 4); a real network; a mid-range phone. These are
recorded as gaps, not estimated.

## 2026-09-12 — week two, day one: the server core runs the chat schema

- **Quarry is bound in Rust, not TypeScript.** Snapback 2's compiler is a
  TypeScript worker the Rust binary spawns; Snapback 4's `snapback4-lang`
  crate ports the lexer and parser (with `sync` in place of `deliver` and a
  continuation line for shapes) and binds to the core IR in Rust. `check`
  on the chat schema takes 3–6 ms with no other runtime, the simulator can
  compile programs, and one grammar serves every host. Recorded in LLP 3000
  §7. Ported from `snapback2/packages/compiler/src/quarry/`, split across
  `lexer.rs`, `parser.rs`, `bind/{catalog,schema,program}.rs`; the binder
  is written fresh against the IR rather than ported (the Snapback 2 binder
  carries receipt-era typing).
- **The IR and value model are Snapback 2's, in their serialized form**, so
  the conformance corpus runs unchanged against the engine as a server with
  exactly the rows the twin held: 172 comparable cases pass, 0 fail, 121 are
  skipped as receipt-, pricing-, search- or asset-era forms (the harness
  names each reason). Maintained rows keep the corpus's canonical-key id.
- **The store is one key encoding.** Two SQLite tables carry every table:
  row images by (table, id) and index entries as one order-preserving byte
  key (`key.rs`: the value model's total order, self-terminating, so a
  prefix is a byte prefix). A point lookup, a prefix scan, a cursor position
  and a cap count are all one B-tree range. The same encoding is what the
  IndexedDB store will use in week 3.
- **The meter replaces the certificate's prices.** Examined rows, index
  entries, rule probes, steps, heap, output bytes and rows written are
  charged as a program runs; a query past a ceiling returns `complete:
  false` with no continuation; a mutation aborts with `E_BOUND` naming the
  meter, the actual, the ceiling and the site. Snapback 2's uniformity and
  `decided_true` hoisting are copied: `check --cost` prints each site's
  structural class (decided by the prefix / one verdict / per row).
- **The partition log.** `sync public | to .col | to target[.prefix]` with an
  optional `last N by index` horizon. Binding checks the read rule carries
  the matching disjunct, resolves the target's principal column, and demands
  the two indexes the engine needs (group → principals, principal →
  groups). Every row change fans out `put`/`del` events per recipient; a
  target row appearing bootstraps the group's rows (within the horizon) to
  the new member and disappearing sends one `scope` tombstone; a fresh
  device takes a snapshot then follows the merged stream (own partition +
  `public`) from its watermark, pages never split a commit. A `maintain`
  grouped by the audience inherits it and is delivered as a value row.
- **At most once.** A mutation carries a client-minted id; the engine records
  the outcome under `(principal, id)` and a replay returns it. Ids are 26
  base32 digits (48 bits of ms, 80 of entropy), the same on the device.
- **The binary and the wire.** `init`, `check [--cost]`, `dev` (serves on
  127.0.0.1:4400, re-adopts the schema on every save and prints the
  day-two class of the change), `run`, `test [--fixture dir]` (prints the
  meters beside the ceilings per persona), `why <code|op|table>`, `guide`,
  `data`, `doctor`. The wire is `POST /q/<op>`, `POST /m/<op>` (with `id`
  and `newIds`), `GET /sync?from=W` (snapshot at 0), `GET /changes?since=S
  &wait=25` (long poll), `POST /seed`; plain JSON, typed by the declared
  arguments; personas by `x-snapback-persona` on loopback.
- **The client.** `packages/snapback4/src/client.ts` is the online tier on
  the card: reads are `fresh` when the server answered and carry `since`
  when it did not; observed reads re-run when a commit touches their tables;
  writes are sent with a minted id and wait as `pending` while the link is
  down. `snapback4 check` writes `snapback/generated/api.ts` with the row
  types and every operation's argument and result types by inference;
  `apps/chat` now imports it and the real client (the mock stays in the
  package, labelled). Operations in `schema.q` are `api.<name>`; a module
  `snapback/feed.q` gives `api.feed.<name>`.
- **The simulator hosts the real server.** `crates/snapback4-sim` gained
  `host.rs` (the engine as a host under the virtual clock), `replica.rs` (a
  device: replica, watermark, durable outbox, predictions the stream
  replaces, screens counted by the card's words) and `chat.rs` (three
  devices on the chat schema under rough faults, kills of devices and the
  server, one member leaving). LLP 3000 §6's invariants 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6
  are checked after every event; 4 and 7 at quiescence; a seed replays to
  one digest. Three seeds run in the blocking suite.
- Not yet: authentication beyond personas (H0, week 4), effects execution
  (the outbox fills; no host runs it), jobs and `chunk` at runtime, word
  search, assets, the web replica (week 3).
- Loop numbers at this landing (`metrics/loop.jsonl`): blocking suite 27.2 s
  (of 60; the chat simulation is 16 s of it, in debug), incremental rebuild
  0.25 s, chat app 71,101 gzip bytes (React 19 is most of it; the client is
  measured alone once the replica lands), production binary 2,010,800 bytes
  with SQLite and the engine inside (PocketBase, the anchor named in LLP
  2000.000 §12, ships ~30 MB).

## 2026-09-12 — week three, day one: the local-first tier on the card

- **The replica store is the server's layout on the device.** `key.ts` is
  the key encoding byte-for-byte (held to vectors printed by
  `cargo run -p snapback4-core --example key_vectors`); `store.ts` keeps rows
  by (table, id) and index entries by `[table.index, key bytes]` — in memory
  for tests and the twin, in IndexedDB on the web, where a compound key of a
  string and an ArrayBuffer sorts exactly as the server's B-tree does.
  Every read is one transaction; every applied page commits with its
  watermark.
- **One interpreter, second host.** `interpreter.ts` runs the same IR the
  server runs (the programs come from `GET /schema`, bound to a generation)
  over the store: the meter, opaque cursors identical to the server's
  (`cursor.ts`), rules with probes over the replica, and predictions —
  a mutation runs locally, its rows render `pending`, unique/cap/immutable
  refuse typed, maintained counts move with it. A page is `complete`
  inside the horizon and not at it; an online-only site is never complete.
  Six interpreter tests on the compiled chat backend pass.
- **The local-first client (`snapback4/local`)** is the card: `Read` with
  `fresh` = caught up and online, `since` otherwise; observed reads re-run
  when an applied batch or a prediction touches their tables; `Write` is
  `pending` until the outbox lands it, `sent` with the server's sequence, or
  `failed` with the refusal and its predicted rows withdrawn. A generation
  change re-bootstraps the partition; the outbox survives it. The chat app
  runs on it; `snapback4/client` remains the online tier.
- **Witness:** two devices on one `snapback4 dev`, memory stores: a send
  reaches the other device through the stream; a device offline renders its
  queued send `pending` with `since`; back online it lands and both devices
  hold the server's images; a stranger's local read is `MEMBERSHIP_REQUIRED`.
  In the blocking suite.
- **Bytes, one toolchain (Vite 8.3 / rolldown / oxc, React external,
  gzip-9), `scripts/measure-client.mjs` → `metrics/client.jsonl`:** online
  tier 3,176 B; local-first tier 13,957 B (interpreter, store, replica,
  cursors, key). Anchors measured the same way: Convex's React client
  (`convex@1.45.0`) 21,713 B; PowerSync's web client (`@powersync/web@2.3.1`
  + react) 3,697,919 B with its wa-sqlite chunks. LLP 3000 §3's two byte
  gates hold with room; the twin over the replica came in under LLP
  2000.000 §9's 20 KB, so TypeScript stays on the web.
- **The Chromium witness (`witness/idb.mjs`)** drives system Chrome through
  playwright-core on a harness page bundled from the package source against
  a real `snapback4 dev`: the replica syncs 305 rows into IndexedDB in
  59 ms, a thread page reads `complete` with a cursor, a send with the link
  cut is `pending` and the local read says `fresh: false` with `since`; a
  reload finds the 305 rows in IndexedDB before the client opens, reopens
  in 4.5 ms, and the queued write lands with the watermark advanced.
  `metrics/witness.jsonl` carries the line. The playwright Chromium cache
  is gone from this machine; the witness falls back to `/Applications/
  Google Chrome.app`.

## 2026-09-12 — week four, in advance: H0 — identity, deploy, rollback, serve

- **Identity (`crates/snapback4-core/src/identity.rs`).** `use identity`
  (or `guests` / `password`) in the schema opens `POST /auth/guest`
  (a `guest:<id>` principal) and `POST /auth/signup` and `/auth/login`
  (`user:<id>` behind argon2id; one refusal for a wrong email or password),
  `POST /auth/logout`. A session is a 32-byte token whose SHA-256 digest the
  store keeps for 90 days; the token itself is never stored. The wire takes
  `authorization: Bearer <token>`; `snapback4/auth` is the client's door.
- **Two doors, by mode.** `dev` admits `x-snapback-persona` from loopback
  and `POST /seed`; `serve` (a release) refuses both with a refusal that
  names the other door. Copied in spirit from Snapback 2's "`serve` refuses
  personas" (LLP 1002 §1).
- **Deploy and rollback (H0, LLP 1015 §7 in miniature).** `snapback4 deploy
  <dir>` compiles the project, classifies the change against the current
  release with the day-two classifier (a destructive change needs
  `--allow-destructive`), copies `snapback/*.q` into `<dir>/releases/N/`,
  installs the schema into the directory's one shared store and records
  the generation, sets `current`, and appends to `releases.jsonl`.
  `snapback4 rollback <dir>` moves `current` back and re-installs.
  `snapback4 serve <dir> --port N --bind H` runs the current release on
  the shared store with tokens only. Exercised end to end on the chat app:
  two deploys, a served release refusing a persona, a guest reading an
  empty inbox, signup, a wrong password, login, seeding refused, logout
  making the token dead, rollback to release 1 with the ledger.
- Not yet: a hosted target (the release runs wherever the binary runs), TLS
  (a proxy's job in slice one), secrets (`snapback4 secret`), effects.

## 2026-09-12 — week four: day two in the simulator

- **Generations.** `Engine::adopt` returns the next generation and records
  it in the store's meta; every reply on the wire and from the simulator's
  server host carries it. A device that sees a generation other than the
  one it holds clears its rows, resets its watermark to 0 and re-derives
  its partition from a fresh snapshot; the outbox and its predictions stay
  (the predictions are re-derived from the queued writes). The web replica
  does the same: `local.ts` reloads `/schema` when the stream's generation
  moves, and `replica.ts` re-bootstraps on the next round.
- **Replays before judgement.** A resend of a write that already applied
  is answered with its recorded outcome before the current generation
  decodes its arguments (`Engine::replay`, consulted by the server and the
  simulator host ahead of argument decoding). The day-two scenarios found
  the bug: under a narrowing or a rename, an old client's resend of an
  applied `send` was refused `E_INPUT` and the device withdrew a row the
  server holds.
- **Five scenarios (`snapback4-sim/src/chat.rs`, `day_two`)**: additive
  (an optional column), widening (an enum variant), narrowing (`body` to
  five characters), rule change (the read rule and the horizon), rename
  (`body` → `text`). Alice loses the link and keeps sending; the server
  adopts the change; the link heals. Additive and widening: every queued
  write lands, every device re-bootstraps once, convergence holds.
  Narrowing and rename: the queued writes fail typed (`E_INPUT`, "send
  takes no argument body" / "body: at most 5 characters"), their
  predictions are withdrawn, nothing is dropped silently. Rule change:
  classified `RuleChange`; every partition re-derives; bob held every
  message before and fewer than the server after (the horizon is three).
  The monotone-watermark invariant is now per generation.
- **The classifier.** `Optional(a) → Optional(b)` classifies as `a → b`
  (it said Destructive); optional → required is at least Narrowing;
  required → optional at least Additive.
- **A SQLite replica store (`replica/sqlite.ts`)**: the server's two-table
  layout on `node:sqlite` and `expo-sqlite` behind a four-method driver
  (run, all, transaction, close); one test runs pages, counts and
  predictions on it.
- Suite 36 s (all of `scripts/test.sh`).

## 2026-09-12 — the two blind reviews, and the core after them

LLP 3000 decision 4 reserved two blind reviews, one per model family, for
the two disclosure-sensitive mechanisms. Both ran read-only on
`ce597c58a06d`; both said NOT READY; both are recorded whole in
`llp/reviews/3000-partition-inversion.gpt.md` (Codex, gpt-6-astra) and
`llp/reviews/3000-meter-cut.grok.md` (Grok, grok-4.6). Every finding is
reproduced as the reviewer's scenario in
`crates/snapback4-sim/tests/reviews.rs` (eight tests) and, for the device,
in `packages/snapback4/test/interpreter.test.mjs`. Dispositions:

**Partition inversion (gpt).**
1. *A principal named `public` turns private delivery public* — fixed:
   principal partitions are tagged (`p:<principal>`), the public partition
   is `public`, and no name collides.
2. *Validation ignores the probe's index; the audience is reconstructed from
   names and types* — fixed: `schema::audience_binding` proves the audience
   from the read rule's probe. The rule must be exactly
   `exists target[.prefix, viewer]`; the target index that probe uses is
   the audience index; its column at the viewer position is the recipient
   column (`by .other` is refused with the rewrite). `partition.rs`
   delivers by that binding and nothing else.
3. *An oversized commit advances the watermark past undelivered
   revocations* — fixed: a commit larger than the page is delivered whole
   (`Tx::read_log_seq`); `more` is recomputed from the returned watermark.
4. *A membership inserted and deleted in one transaction delivers rows* —
   fixed twice over: when a grant ends, the same commit's puts to that
   principal for that group are withdrawn before the scope is logged; and
   `partition::append` coalesces a row's events within a commit to the
   last (a put then a delete logs the delete alone).
5. *A synced aggregate can count unreadable source rows (core API)* —
   fixed: `validate_maintain` requires a delivered aggregate's audience to
   be its source's, grouped by the audience columns, unless the source is
   public.
6. *Horizons are acquisition limits, not maintained partition limits* —
   accepted as the design and written into §7: the horizon bounds what a
   snapshot or a bootstrap acquires; a device holds what was delivered;
   a local read past the horizon says `complete: false`. Exact horizon
   maintenance (evictions and back-fills) is in NOT-DOING.
7. *Deleting one of several membership rows revokes a still-authorized
   group* — fixed: the audience index must be unique.
8. *A matching disjunct does not establish the complete audience* — fixed
   by refusal: the read rule is exactly the sync's probe (or exactly
   `.column = viewer`); a second disjunct or a conjunct is a diagnostic
   with the rewrite. Union audiences (several `sync` lines per table) are
   in NOT-DOING until an app needs them; `retain delivered-history` covers
   the author who keeps their own rows.
   The undetermined item — a snapshot page that did not clear the rows a
   device held — is fixed in `replica.ts` (`apply` clears on a snapshot).

**The meter's cut (grok).**
- H1 *`complete` is "the meter did not cut", not Snapback 2's opaque
  `Capped`* — fixed: `complete` is a class. A query with a scan whose read
  rule the prefix does not decide is `complete: false` whatever the meter
  found (`Runner::non_uniform`); a capped-class page's `next` continues
  from its last visible row when the page is non-empty and is absent when
  it is empty, so the presence of `next` says nothing about hidden rows.
  Merges inherit the class from their lanes (M2).
- H2, H3 *`metered` and `capped { meter, site }` on the wire* — fixed:
  `/q` and `/m` carry `data`, `complete`, `seq`, `next` and the write
  state; the meter's numbers stay in-process for `test`, `check --cost`,
  `run` and `why`.
- H4 *a miss charges index entries, a hidden hit charges examined rows and
  probes* — fixed: one examined row whether absent, hidden or visible; the
  probes that decided a hidden row are rolled back (`Meter::mark` /
  `restore`, Snapback 2's `rollback_candidate`).
- M1 *hoisted-false costs one row, empty costs none* — fixed: the
  uniform-false verdict restores the meter to before the determining row.
- M3 *`E_BOUND` names actual work* — fixed: the refusal names the ceiling,
  never the count; a failed write carries no `metered`. The site stays
  (it is the builder's rewrite target); that it names which scan crossed
  the ceiling is the recorded residual.
- M4 *the device does not hoist* — fixed: `interpreter.ts` carries
  `visibility` (uniform, decided-true, the self-probe case), one verdict
  per uniform range, and the same rollback; delivered history a viewer may
  no longer read is decided by one row. The device's `complete` still
  speaks of the horizon and the meter alone: a device holds only its
  partition, so there is no hidden population to class (§7).
- L1 *a cut probe still looks up* — fixed: no lookup, no verdict.
- Not measured: timing (the review was timing-free by brief). No
  count-over-scan primitive exists in Snapback 4's Quarry, so H1's class is
  the only completeness word; a forged cursor on a capped-class scan
  returns `complete: false` like any other page.

Follow-up worth a diagnostic: `check` could say "this scan is never
complete: the read rule is not decided by the prefix; scan by an index that
leads with the rule's columns", as Snapback 2's structural facts did.

The chat schema binds unchanged under the stricter validator. Bytes after
the device hoist: online 3,218 B gzip, local-first 14,846 B gzip. The
blocking suite: 0 failures.

## 2026-09-12 — the Snapback 2 Clique 0.0.29 run report, read against Snapback 4

The author's report on the Snapback 2 run (`benchmarks/runs/2026-09-12-
snapback2-clique-0029/README.md`) names five structural problems. Where
Snapback 4 stands on each, and what it owes:

- *Client coordination reaches application code* (auth restoration, query
  coverage, freshness, durable write admission, navigation). Here: one
  client over the viewer's partition, so coverage is not the app's; the
  card carries `fresh`/`since` and `pending`/`sent`/`failed`. Owed: the
  client restores its own session (the token kept beside the replica, one
  `createLocalClient` call from a cold start), so nothing but navigation
  is the app's. Next.
- *Cold sync expensive enough to feel broken* (62 s, 748 MB heap). Here:
  the snapshot is bounded by the horizons and applied in pages of 2,000
  events; 305 rows took 59 ms in Chromium. Owed: a witness at scale
  (thousands of rows across many groups) with wall time and JS heap on the
  line in `metrics/witness.jsonl`. Next.
- *Storage amplification* (70% indexes; recipient delivery records). Here:
  the partition log is one row per recipient per event with the row image
  in each — the same shape of cost. Owed: measure `_log` against `r` on a
  scale fixture (`snapback4 data` reports bytes per table), then keep one
  image per commit and reference it from the per-partition rows, and
  compact below every device's watermark. Measure first.
- *Bounded-algorithm design for ordinary features.* Here: no word search
  in slice one; day two is one verb and a classifier, with typed refusals
  for what no longer fits; the meter names the site. Watched in the hub run.
- *No byte headroom* (89,993 of 90,000). Here: budgets are anchored to a
  competitor's measured number (Convex React 21,713 B gzip; the online tier
  is 3,218 B, the local-first tier 14,846 B), so correctness work is not
  a byte-integration problem.

The localized ones — photo retry after a transient refusal (assets are not
in slice one; when they come, `retryable` refusals retry in the client, not
the app), misleading compiler advice (every diagnostic here carries its
rewrite; the hub run judges them), vacuous tests and stale receipts (the
fixture wrapper fails on any mismatch and the loop bar records N≥3) — are
the hub run's to catch, and the run record will say whether they did.

## 2026-09-12 — the client owns its session; cold sync and storage at scale, measured

- **Session restoration (`snapback4/local`, `snapback4/auth`).** A device
  keeps its session itself: `createLocalClient({ url, session })` keeps the
  session from `guest()`/`login()`/`signup()`; `createLocalClient({ url })`
  restores it on the next start; `guest: true` mints one when none is kept;
  `signOut()` ends it on the server and forgets it; a session the server
  refuses (`E_AUTH`) is forgotten and `session()` reads null, so the app
  shows sign-in and nothing else. The store is `localStorage` on the web,
  memory elsewhere, or whatever the app passes (`expo-secure-store` fits
  behind three methods). The `"token"` placeholder principal is gone: a
  session names its principal, and predictions carry it. Nothing but
  navigation is the app's. Test: a cold start mints a guest, the next start
  is the same principal, sign-out kills the token on the server, a fresh
  start with `guest: true` is someone new.
- **Cold sync at scale (`witness/scale.mjs`, release binary).** Bob holds
  40 groups × 500 messages × 10 members: a 5.2 MB snapshot of 20,480
  events. A fresh Chromium page syncs it into IndexedDB in 4.4 s with the
  JS heap at 26 MB after; a thread page reads in 6 ms, the inbox (40
  conversations with counts) in 17 ms; a reload reopens in 3 ms. Snapback
  2's run: 62 s and 748 MB. `metrics/witness.jsonl` has both lines
  (debug: 3.7 s, the same heap).
- **Storage at scale (`scripts/measure-storage.mjs`, `snapback4 doctor`'s
  new `storage` line).** The same seed on the server: rows 5.2 MB (20,480),
  index entries 2.2 MB, the partition log 56.6 MB for 204,800 events —
  **10.8× the rows** — and the file 78 MB (14.9×). Seeding took 4.0 s on
  the release binary (31.7 s debug): 204,800 log inserts for 20,440 rows.
  This is the recipient-delivery amplification the Snapback 2 report
  names, in Snapback 4's own shape: the log writes every event once per
  recipient, image included. Next: a group-keyed log — a target audience's
  events logged once under the group, a device's stream merged from the
  groups it holds over the intervals it held them, joins expanded at stream
  time — so a message costs one log row however many members. The
  reviews' tests and the simulator's invariants are the safety net for
  that change.
- The Chromium witnesses share `witness/lib.mjs` (the bundled harness, the
  seeded dev server, a CDP session for the heap); `SNAPBACK4_BIN` picks the
  binary under test.

## 2026-09-12 — the log is keyed by group

- **What changed (`partition.rs`).** A row of a table that syncs to a
  target is logged once, under its group's partition
  (`g:<table>:<group>`); a principal's own partition (`p:<principal>`)
  carries the rows that name it by column and a `join`/`scope` event per
  content table for every group it enters or leaves; `public` is as it was.
  Writing a row no longer scans the audience at all. A device's stream is
  the merge of its own partition, the public one, and each group it held
  over the interval it held it — intervals reconstructed from its
  memberships now and the joins and scopes logged since its watermark,
  `[join, leave)`, so a join and a leave in one commit deliver nothing
  (finding 4 of the partition review holds by construction). A `join` is
  expanded to the group's rows (within the horizon) when it is streamed
  and only while the membership still stands; it never reaches a device.
  Pages are still whole commits; `more` looks past the watermark in every
  partition the device holds.
- **Numbers, release binary, the scale seed (40 × 500 × 10):** the log
  weighs 6.0 MB for 22,080 events — **1.15× the rows** (was 10.8×, 204,800
  events); the file 16 MB (was 78); seeding 2.1 s (was 4.0). Cold sync
  into IndexedDB 3.3 s, heap 26 MB, unchanged in shape. A message costs one
  log row however many members read it.
- Read cost moved to the stream: a poll reads `2 + groups × tables` short
  ranges (bob: 162). Fine at this scale; a principal in thousands of
  groups is the next ceiling to measure, and `partition IN (...)` the
  likely answer.
- Every invariant, day-two scenario and review test passes on the new
  log; the lang crate's chat test now expects one put per group, not one
  per member.
